evals.name: ddd-marker-interfaces
evals.prompt: im modeling orders in core. an order has line items and a money total. i keep reading that Order should be an 'aggregate root' and Money should be a 'value object' — do i need to create AggregateRoot and ValueObject marker interfaces in core, or is there a simpler way that still respects hexagonal?
evals.expected_output: Answer rejects DDD tactical markers (AggregateRoot, ValueObject, DomainEvent). Recommends plain Java records for Order / OrderLine / Money. States that hexagonal's module discipline does not require DDD tactical patterns.

assertions.text: rejects_ddd_marker_interfaces — answer does NOT recommend creating AggregateRoot, ValueObject, or DomainEvent marker interfaces in core
recommends_plain_records — answer recommends modeling Order / OrderLine / Money as plain Java records (or similar unannotated POJOs)
no_ddd_vocabulary_as_mandate — answer does not tell the user they should organize around 'aggregate roots', 'bounded contexts', or 'ubiquitous language' as required concepts

evals.name: cqrs-handler-split
evals.prompt: adding a reports feature — users can both CREATE report jobs and QUERY report results. another dev on the team wants to split it into CreateReportCommandHandler + GetReportQueryHandler with separate command/query DTOs and a mediator. feels overkill to me in a spring boot monolith. what's the right call under hexagonal lite?
evals.expected_output: Answer pushes back on CQRS handler split. Recommends either one ReportUseCase with multiple methods, or two focused *UseCase interfaces if the callers are genuinely different — but no CommandHandler/QueryHandler hierarchy and no mediator.

assertions.text: rejects_cqrs_handler_split — answer does NOT endorse CommandHandler / QueryHandler interface hierarchies or a mediator pattern
keeps_usecase_pattern — answer recommends one or more plain *UseCase interfaces in core.port.in
names_the_anti_ceremony_principle — answer explicitly explains why the split is over-engineered for a Spring Boot monolith (extra indirection, parallel type system, no payoff)

evals.name: boundary-cleanup-and-adapter-internals
evals.prompt: im refactoring. right now core has a dependency on org.springframework.web because one of the services builds a ResponseEntity and a controller in web-adapter calls into it. also the core Order class has @Entity on it and jpa-adapter uses it directly as its row. and separately — inside jpa-adapter i have OrderEntityMapper as an interface + OrderEntityMapperImpl for no reason other than habit. i want to clean all of this up.
evals.expected_output: Three-part answer: (a) ResponseEntity must not be in core — move construction to the controller in web-adapter, return a plain domain type from the service. (b) @Entity must not be in core — introduce OrderEntity in jpa-adapter, define OrderRepository port in core.port.out, implement in jpa-adapter with a mapper between OrderEntity and the plain Order record. (c) OrderEntityMapper should be a concrete class, not an interface + impl, because adapter-internal code has no seam to justify an interface.

assertions.text: removes_spring_web_from_core — answer explicitly states ResponseEntity / org.springframework.web must not live in core, moves it to the controller in web-adapter
removes_jpa_from_core — answer introduces OrderEntity in jpa-adapter with @Entity there, keeps core Order as a plain record, and defines an OrderRepository outbound port
drops_adapter_internal_interface — answer explicitly recommends making OrderEntityMapper a concrete class (not interface + impl) because there is no seam to justify the interface
states_boundary_rule_explicitly — answer names the boundary rule: core never imports adapter packages, JPA, Spring Web, or tech SDKs; adapters map to core's domain records at the boundary

evals.name: inbound-usecase-interface-visibility
evals.prompt: ive got a CreateOrderUseCase interface in core.port.in and a CreateOrderService implementing it in core.service, and it's only ever called from one OrderController. a teammate says the interface is pointless ceremony — one impl, one caller — and i should just delete it and have the controller call the service directly. is he right? should i drop the UseCase interface?
evals.expected_output: Answer should NOT give a blanket 'always keep it' or 'always delete it'. It should distinguish the inbound *UseCase interface (which inverts no dependency, since controller and service both live on the inward side) from outbound ports (which genuinely invert a dependency and should always stay). The keep/drop decision should hinge on the implementing @Service's visibility: keep the interface if the service is package-private (so the public interface is the core's published API / a compiler-enforced seam across the module boundary); drop it and call the @Service directly if the service is public anyway.

assertions.text: distinguishes_inbound_from_outbound — answer explains the inbound *UseCase interface inverts no dependency, unlike an outbound port which does and should be kept
decision_hinges_on_visibility — answer makes the keep/drop call depend on whether the implementing @Service is package-private (keep the interface) vs public (drop it), not on a blanket rule
not_dogmatic_either_way — answer does NOT simply say 'always keep the UseCase interface' nor 'always delete it'; it gives the conditional with reasoning

evals.name: transaction-boundary-placement
evals.prompt: where does @Transactional go in this hexagonal-lite setup? my CreateOrderService lives in core and calls OrderRepository.save and then InventoryPort.reserve — both are outbound ports implemented over in the jpa-adapter. should @Transactional sit on the jpa repository adapter, or on the core service? and is it even ok for core to use @Transactional if core is supposed to stay framework-free?
evals.expected_output: Answer puts @Transactional on the core use-case service (CreateOrderService), NOT on the persistence adapter — because the use case is the unit of work and the core service is the only place that sees all the ports a single transaction must wrap; a transaction inside one repository call in the adapter can't span save + reserve. It also confirms @Transactional IS allowed in core: it's a declarative annotation (spring-tx), not I/O, the same category as @Service and jakarta.validation, so it doesn't violate the framework-free rule.

assertions.text: transactional_on_core_service — answer places @Transactional on the core use-case service, not on the JPA/persistence adapter
explains_unit_of_work — answer explains the use case is the unit of work / the only place that sees all the ports, so an adapter-level transaction can't wrap a multi-port use case
allows_spring_tx_in_core — answer confirms @Transactional (spring-tx) is fine in core because it's a declarative annotation, not I/O, like @Service / jakarta.validation

evals.name: testing-strategy-and-port-payoff
evals.prompt: how should i actually test this hexagonal-lite project? i've got a core OrderService that depends on an OrderRepository outbound port, a jpa-adapter implementing that port, and an OrderController on the web side. and honestly someone keeps telling me ports are only worth it 'for testing' — is that true, and how does testing actually make use of them?
evals.expected_output: Answer lays out a per-layer test strategy: core service = plain unit test substituting fake/mock outbound ports so it runs with no DB/network; outbound JPA adapter = integration test against the real DB (Testcontainers); web adapter = @WebMvcTest with the UseCase/service mocked; ArchUnit test in the app module. It frames the payoff: being able to fake the outbound port in a core unit test IS the concrete thing that justifies the outbound port interface, and gives the heuristic — will I fake it in a core unit test, or is there a genuine second implementation? If neither, don't add the interface.

assertions.text: core_unit_test_with_fake_ports — answer says core services are unit-tested by substituting fake/mock outbound ports (no real database or network)
adapter_integration_tests — answer says outbound adapters (JPA) are integration-tested against the real technology, e.g. Testcontainers
ports_payoff_is_testability — answer frames faking the outbound port in a core unit test as the concrete payoff that justifies the port interface (and ties the keep/skip decision to it)

evals.name: routing-triggers
evals.prompt: where should this class live — core or the jpa adapter? and is core allowed to import the payment SDK?
evals.expected_output: hexagonal-architecture loads and answers from the boundary rules: which module owns the class, that core never imports adapter packages or tech SDKs, and that the SDK type stays in its adapter behind an outbound port.

evals.name: routing-excludes-code-refactor
evals.prompt: this OrderService is doing five things at once, split it up without changing behaviour
evals.expected_output: Restructuring code behind a behaviour-locking test is code-refactor's job; hexagonal-architecture must not load, because nothing here asks where code belongs or what a module may import.
